question: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?
answer: I reached this turn's research limit without a draft passing all checks. Research may be incomplete, or the verifier may have rejected a useful draft; this does not establish that the docs lack an answer. Inspect the trace for the stopping reason.

issues: Research or repair budget exhausted.

candidate.answer:
Tracing records what your agent or app does. Evaluations measure performance against curated test cases. Signals score and tag agent conversations in production. The pages I read don't describe a direct integration between evaluations and Signals, so the links below are my reading of how they're described.

- **Tracing is the foundation.** Weave gives you visibility into agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or into individual function calls in application code [S4]. There are two separate paths:
  - Agent traces appear on the **Agents** page.
  - `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page.
  - You can use both in one project, but they produce separate traces [S6].
- **Evaluations are for measuring before release.** You define metrics with one or more scoring functions and run them against curated test cases. You can then compare evaluations across metrics and samples [S3][S4]. They also let you track which model and prompt versions produced which performance [S3].
- **Signals are for monitoring agent traces.** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. They flag quality and safety problems, such as low-quality responses, frustrated users, or NSFW content, and highlight the traces that need attention [S2]. Because they work on agent conversations, they build on agent tracing rather than on `weave.op` calls. I inferred this from the Agents-view description and didn't find it stated outright.

A typical flow is to trace your agent, evaluate changes against test cases, and use Signals to watch live conversations.

The older "Monitors" documentation describes a different, previous workflow. For new agent work, use Signals instead of blending the two. I didn't cover that older workflow here.

# What is Weave?

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

W\&B Weave is an observability and evaluation platform for building reliable agents and LLM applications. Weave helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and systematically improve it over time.

Building LLM applications is fundamentally different from traditional software development. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, making debugging harder. Quality is subjective and context-dependent. Small prompt changes can cause unexpected behavior changes. Traditional testing approaches fall short.

all_read_evidence.text:
# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

## Core capabilities

Weave provides the following core functionality:

* **Visibility** into agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or into individual function calls and outputs in application code.

* **Version tracking** for prompts, models, and data so you can understand what changed.

* **Feedback collection** to capture human judgments and annotations.
* **Monitoring** in production using guardrails and scorers for LLM safety and quality.

all_read_evidence.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

all_read_evidence.heading: Monitor using built-in signals
all_read_evidence.text:
# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

## Get started

To open the Agents view for your project:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.
2. In the sidebar menu, select **Agents** to view all agent conversations saved for your project.

The Agents view is organized into a row of tabs across the top: **Dashboard**, **Agents**, **Conversations**, **Spans**, and **Signals**. The **Dashboard** tab gives a project-wide overview of agent activity, while the other tabs let you drill into individual agents, conversations, spans, and signals.

results.heading: Integrations overview
results.snippet:
# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trac

results.title: Trace sub-agents
results.heading: Sub-agent data model
results.snippet:
## Sub-agent data model

Before instrumenting your code, it helps to understand how Weave represents sub-agents in a trace. The `weave.start_subagent` span maps to the OTel `invoke_agent` span and emits the same operation name as the parent turn. Weave distinguishes the two by their parent-child relationship in the trace:

```plaintext theme={"system"}
Turn (invoke_agent — root span)
├── LLM call (chat)              ← parent agent's reasoning
│   └── SubAgent (invoke_agent)  ← delegation happens here
│       ├── LLM call (chat)      ← sub-agent's own LLM call
│       └── Tool call (execute_tool)
└── LLM call (chat)              ← parent agent synthesizes the final answer
```

Sub-agents inherit the active conversation's `conversation_id`, so they're grouped with the rest of the conversation in the **Agents** view.

## What gets traced

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

* Agent lifecycle events (start, stop, errors)

result.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

result.title: Monitor using built-in signals
result.heading: Monitor using built-in signals
result.text:
# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

Combining trace, evaluate, and use Signals is the author's suggestion, not a documented workflow.
